nameStory: This microscopic algae doesn't have a common name since it's invisible to the naked eye! Scientists named it Micrasterias mahabuleshwarensis after Mahabaleshwar, a hill station in India where it was first discovered. The genus name Micrasterias means 'little star' in Greek, referring to the beautiful star-like shape these tiny organisms display under a microscope.
description: This is a single-celled freshwater algae that you'll never see without a microscope - each cell is only about 50-100 micrometers wide (thinner than a human hair). Under magnification, it looks like an intricate green snowflake or star, with a flattened, symmetrical shape divided into two mirror-image halves. The cell has elaborate lobes and projections that radiate outward, creating one of nature's most beautiful geometric patterns. Despite being just one cell, it's a complex living organism that can photosynthesize like plants.

idTips.label: Star-like symmetry
idTips.description: The cell is perfectly symmetrical, split down the middle with identical halves that mirror each other like folded paper - this bilateral symmetry is key to identifying all Micrasterias species

idTips.label: Elaborate lobing pattern
idTips.description: The cell edges are deeply divided into multiple lobes and sub-lobes, creating an ornate, lace-like appearance that's more complex than simple round algae

idTips.label: Flattened shape
idTips.description: When viewed from the side under a microscope, the cell appears thin and flat like a coin rather than spherical

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: The cell appears bright green due to chlorophyll, the same pigment that makes plants green

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Cells measure roughly 50-100 micrometers across - about the width of a very fine human hair

habitat: Found in clean, soft-water ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, particularly in acidic bog waters and mountain ponds. These algae prefer nutrient-poor waters and are often indicators of good water quality. You'll need to collect water samples from these habitats and examine them under a microscope to observe these organisms.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures warm and daylight increases, making this a good time to find them in freshwater samples.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when populations are most abundant and active, dividing frequently in warm, sunny conditions.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may decline as temperatures drop and light decreases, though some may persist in warmer protected waters.
seasonality.winter: Populations are at their lowest, with many cells going dormant or dying back, though some may survive under ice in deeper waters.

funFact: Each Micrasterias cell is like a living work of art that takes hours to create - when the cell divides, each half must slowly grow back its missing mirror image over 12-24 hours, rebuilding its intricate star pattern lobe by lobe with mathematical precision!
confusionNotes: Under a microscope, it can be confused with other ornate desmid algae, but Micrasterias species are distinguished by their flat, star-like shape with bilateral symmetry - remember 'Micrasterias = micro stars' to recall their characteristic radiating, symmetrical pattern.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England with only 13 recorded observations, making it a special find for microscopists. Originally described from India, its presence here shows how these microscopic organisms can have surprisingly wide global distributions despite being invisible to us.
compareHints: Micrasterias mahabuleshwarensis differs from its relatives by having a specific pattern of lobing and cell proportions that require expert examination to distinguish. Compared to other Micrasterias species like M. truncata or M. radiosa, it has its own unique 'fingerprint' of lobe shapes and sizes. All Micrasterias species share the same basic star-like, bilaterally symmetrical form, but each has subtle differences in their ornate edge patterns.
